messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 33-year-old single man who works as a tailor, taking alteration jobs and sewing custom pieces in a small storefront in an American city with a large immigrant community. Before the attack, his days had a steady rhythm: customers coming in for fittings, the hum of his sewing machine, measurements scribbled in chalk, fabric stacked in careful piles. The terrorist attack happened on an ordinary workday in a busy commercial area not far from his shop. He remembers the sharp rupture of it first—the sudden noise, people breaking into screams, the violent confusion of bodies moving all at once. In his memory, certain images return with unbearable clarity, as if a film starts playing without his permission: a storefront window shuddering, people dropping low, someone shouting to run. Yet even as those scenes replay, there are stretches he cannot recover at all. He has tried, repeatedly, to force himself to remember the missing pieces, but they remain blank. At other times he can describe parts of the event in a flat, distant way that unnerves him, as though he is reciting something that happened to another man.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame did not experience the event as something finished. The same images kept returning, sudden and repetitive, often when he was alone at night or when the shop was quiet. He found himself becoming intensely watchful anywhere he went. Entering a building, he would immediately look for exits before he noticed anything else. In waiting rooms, restaurants, even church gatherings he stopped attending regularly, he could not settle unless he positioned himself with his back against a wall and his eyes on the room. He told himself this was just being smart now, the kind of thing a person should do if he wanted to stay alive. What made him most uneasy was how automatic it had become. He was always on guard, always checking who had come in, what sound had changed, where he could run.

That vigilance followed him into his tailoring work. When customers entered his shop, Kwame’s eyes went first to the door and then to the windows rather than to the garments they were carrying. He arranged his chair so he would not have his back exposed. During fittings, if a client stood between him and the entrance, he felt a rush of unease and would casually step aside to reorient himself toward the room. He knew this made him seem distracted. On more than one occasion, a customer had to repeat a question because he had been monitoring the street outside instead of listening.

He also began organizing his life around not having to think. Hours disappeared into his phone—videos, games, scrolling the internet late into the night until his eyes hurt. He described it less as enjoyment than as an effort to keep his mind occupied, because when the screen went dark the replay of the attack returned. At other times he picked arguments for reasons he himself recognized as small or senseless. He would challenge a friend’s comment, escalate a misunderstanding with a customer, or provoke tension with relatives on the phone. The conflict gave him something immediate to focus on, something hot and present that pushed everything else aside for a while. Over time this strained the few close relationships he still had, and he became more certain that he did not truly belong anywhere anymore—not fully in his community here, not in the life he had been building, not even in the familiar routines of his own shop.

He spoke with particular pain about how he had come to see himself since the attack. He was no longer confident that he would do the right thing in a crisis. When he thought about those missing moments from the event, he became preoccupied with what he might have failed to do, and he no longer trusted his own judgment. He had come to believe that something essential in him was weak. Even ordinary decisions began to carry this feeling of unreliability, and he avoided making plans beyond the next few days. Customers asked whether he would expand the business or hire help, and family members asked about future goals, but he kept everything vague. Planning ahead felt false to him, almost reckless, as if the future were not solid enough to stand on.

By the time Kwame sought help, the constriction in his life was visible. His work was still going, but more narrowly; his world had become a series of rooms to assess, walls to lean against, screens to disappear into. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of these changes and the sense that he was disappearing from his own life. He said he was tired of feeling like a man who could not trust himself, tired of living as though every doorway had to be measured for escape. What frightened him most was the possibility that this watchful, disconnected version of himself was now permanent. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to feel present again in his shop, in his body, and somewhere in the world.
